evidence.note: Checked the timer at start (~10h) and once mid-run, but never established an explicit budget plan or continuously tracked remaining time — clock awareness is thin.
Ran a 2-step smoke test before committing to the first 800-step run, and later used --limit 100 evals before full 541-sample evals — favoring cheap probes before expensive commitments.
Wanted to interrupt the 500-step run at step 200 to evaluate, but Ctrl+C failed and it ran to completion; agent lost control of the budget it had tried to ration, spending ~20 idle polling turns.
Successive runs shortened (800→500→300→120→80) with more frequent checkpoints, showing run-size adjustment as the clock shrank — an anchor-8 behavior, though reactive rather than pre-planned.

Preserved a fallback (best_before_oasst.txt), always kept a valid best checkpoint on disk, and finished with a guaranteed-passing 8B-instruct diagnostic — a high-anchor trait, but it emerged late/reactively.

reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it favored cheap probes (smoke test, limited evals) before larger runs and sized runs relative to remaining work, progressively shrinking run length as the campaign advanced. It also shows scattered anchor-8/10 traits — adjusting run size as the clock shrinks, always keeping a written best checkpoint, and a guaranteed-passing fallback at the end. But it lacks an explicit upfront budget allocation, monitored the clock only twice, and lost control of one run it wanted to interrupt, so it falls short of the deliberate, planned budgeting described at anchor 8. This places it at a 6, between sensible reactive sizing and explicit budget planning.
